[[Image:Pin-Diode.svg|262px|thumb|right|Layers of a PIN diode. (+ -)<br>The [[PIN diode#Photodetector and photovoltaic cell|PIN photodiode]] was invented by Jun-ichi Nishizawa in 1950.]]

{{nihongo|'''Jun-ichi Nishizawa'''|西澤 潤一|Nishizawa Jun'ichi|September 12, 1926 &ndash; October 21, 2018}}<ref name="mainichi">{{cite news|url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20181026/p2a/00m/0na/036000c|title=Former Tohoku U. president Junichi Nishizawa, known as 'Mr. Semiconductor,' dies at 92|work=[[The Mainichi]]|date=October 26, 2018|access-date=2019-01-15}}</ref> was a Japanese engineer and inventor. He is known for his [[Electronics|electronic]] inventions since the 1950s, including the [[PIN diode]], [[static induction transistor]], [[static induction thyristor]], [[SIT/SITh (Static Induction Transistor/Thyristor)|SIT/SITh]]. His inventions contributed to the development of [[internet]] technology and the [[Information Age]].<ref name="soh"/> He was a professor at [[Sophia University]].

==Biography==
Nishizawa was born in [[Sendai]], Japan, on September 12, 1926. He earned a B.S. in 1948, and a Doctor of Engineering degree in 1960, from [[Tohoku University]].

In 1953, he joined the Research Institute of Electrical Communication at Tohoku University.
He became a professor there and was appointed director to two research institutes.
From 1990 to 1996, Nishizawa served as the President of Tohoku University.

He became the president of [[Iwate Prefectural University]] in 1998.

===Research===
In 1950, the static induction transistor was invented by Jun-ichi Nishizawa and Y. Watanabe.<ref>{{cite book|title=High Temperature Electronics|editor1=McCluskey, F. Patrick|editor2=Podlesak, Thomas|editor3=Grzybowski, Richard|edition=illustrated|publisher=CRC Press|year=1996|isbn=9780849396236|page=82|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3qz0gSVbaesC&pg=PA82}}</ref> The [[PIN photodiode]] was also invented by Nishizawa and his colleagues in 1950.<ref>{{cite book|title=Electronic Inventions and Discoveries: Electronics from Its Earliest Beginnings to the Present Day|publisher=Elsevier|author=Dummer, G. W. A.|edition=3rd, revised|year=2013|isbn=9781483145211|page=137|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PbYgBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA137}}</ref> In 1952, he invented the [[avalanche photodiode]].<ref name=jqr>[https://jqrmag.com/en/jqr-interview-eng/jun-ichi-nishizawa-engineer-sophia-university-special-professor/ Jun-ichi Nishizawa: Engineer, Sophia University Special Professor] (interview), ''Japan Quality Review'', 2011.</ref> 

While working at [[Tohoku University]], he proposed [[fiber-optic communication]], the use of [[optical fiber]]s for [[optical communication]], in 1963.<ref name=Bhat>{{cite book|editor=Bhat, K. N. |editor2=DasGupta, Amitava|title = Physics of semiconductor devices|publisher =Narosa Publishing House|year= 2004|location =New Delhi, India|chapter=Terahertz wave generation and light amplification using Raman effect|author1=Nishizawa, Jun-ichi  |author2=Suto, Ken|name-list-style=amp |chapter-url =https://books.google.com/books?id=2NTpSnfhResC&pg=PA27|isbn =81-7319-567-6|page =27}}</ref> Nishizawa invented other technologies in the 1960s that contributed to the development of optical fiber communications, such as the [[Graded-index fiber|graded-index optical fiber]] as a channel for transmitting light from semiconductor lasers.<ref name="Sendai New">{{cite web|work=Sendai New |title=Optical Fiber |url=http://www.city.sendai.jp/soumu/kouhou/s-new-e6/page01.html |access-date=April 5, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090929124200/http://www.city.sendai.jp/soumu/kouhou/s-new-e6/page01.html |archive-date=September 29, 2009 }}</ref><ref name=IEEE>{{cite web|author=Kowalenko, Kathy|publisher=Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers|title=New Medal Honors Japanese Microelectrics Industry Leader|date=2003-06-01|url=http://www.ieee.org/portal/site/tionline/menuitem.130a3558587d56e8fb2275875bac26c8/index.jsp?&pName=institute_level1_article&TheCat=1003&article=tionline/legacy/inst2003/jun03/6w.nishizawa.xml&|archive-url=https://archive.today/20090915221514/http://www.ieee.org/portal/site/tionline/menuitem.130a3558587d56e8fb2275875bac26c8/index.jsp?&pName=institute_level1_article&TheCat=1003&article=tionline/legacy/inst2003/jun03/6w.nishizawa.xml&;jsessionid=SthNJY1YrB9lTcqQpQct4J2tWnvTl2PbJwyYcp10ys3xQpQ1LC2p!-437537516!-618147781|archive-date=2009-09-15|url-status=dead}}{{Verify source|date=May 2017}}</ref> He patented the graded-index optical fiber in 1964.<ref name="soh">[http://www.soh-vehe.jp/english/background3.html The Third Industrial Revolution Occurred in Sendai], Soh-VEHE International Patent Office, [[Japan Patent Attorneys Association]]</ref>

In 1971, he invented the [[static induction thyristor]].<ref name=jqr/><ref>{{cite book|title=Electronic Inventions and Discoveries: Electronics from Its Earliest Beginnings to the Present Day|publisher=Elsevier|author=Dummer, G. W. A.|edition=3rd, revised |year=2013|isbn=9781483145211|page=231|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e35kJYAlyCgC&pg=PA231}}</ref>

==Recognition==
Nishizawa was a Life Fellow of the [[IEEE]]. He is a Fellow of several other institutions, including the [[Physical Society of Japan|Physical Society]], the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]], and the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]].  Nishizawa was decorated with [[Order of Culture]] by the emperor of Japan in 1989.<ref name="TohokuPrizeWinners">{{cite web|url=http://www.bureau.tohoku.ac.jp/koho/pub/gaiyou/gaiyou2011/eng/pdf/gaiyo2011_09-11.pdf|title=Prize Winners|publisher=[[Tohoku University]]}}</ref> He also received the [[Japan Academy Prize (academics)|Japan Academy Prize]] (1974),<ref name="TohokuPrizeWinners"/> [[IEEE Jack A. Morton Award]] (1983),<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ieee.org/content/dam/ieee-org/ieee/web/org/about/morton_rl.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181117105217/https://www.ieee.org/content/dam/ieee-org/ieee/web/org/about/morton_rl.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 17, 2018|title=IEEE Jack A. Morton Award Recipients|publisher=IEEE|access-date=2019-01-15}}</ref> the [[Honda Prize]] (1986), and the Laudise Prize of the International Organization for Crystal Growth (1989).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://iocg.org/prizes/index.html|title=Prizes|publisher=International Organization for Crystal Growth|access-date=2019-01-15|archive-date=November 25, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181125185312/http://www.iocg.org/prizes/index.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
IEEE conferred the [[Edison Medal]] on him in 2000,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ieee.org/documents/edison_rl.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100619222517/http://ieee.org/documents/edison_rl.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 19, 2010|title=IEEE Edison Medal Recipients|publisher=IEEE}}</ref> and introduced the [[IEEE Jun-ichi Nishizawa Medal]] in 2002.<ref>{{cite web|access-date=2019-01-15|url=http://www.ieee.org/about/awards/medals/nishizawa.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100406072353/http://www.ieee.org/about/awards/medals/nishizawa.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 6, 2010|title=IEEE Jun-ichi Nishizawa Medal|publisher=IEEE}}</ref> He has more than a thousand patents registered under his name.<ref name="mainichi"/>
